newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croats bury victim of Serb massacre at Ovcara.
newsitem.headline: Croats bury victim of Serb massacre at Ovcara.

text.p: Five years and three months after he was executed by Serb forces at Ovcara with 199 other patients of Vukovar hospital, the remains of Tomislav Lesic were buried in an emotional funeral in Zagreb on Friday.

Lesic, a Zagreb pharmacist who volunteered for the national guard to defend Vukovar in the summer of 1991 at the age of 41, was the first victim of the Ovcara massacre to be identified by family members on Monday.

Last year the expert team of the U.N. Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia unearthed 200 bodies from Ovcara farm, a few kilometres south of the town of Vukovar in the Serb-held enclave of Eastern Slavonia.
They identified 60 sets of remains in January, confirming most of the victims were hospital patients.
Ten out of 11 families, summoned this week to confirm the tribunal's preliminary identification, accepted its findings. The procedure is expected to take two weeks.
"We have problems with one family which did not accept the identification," government Minister Ivica Kostovic told Reuters on Friday, giving no other details.
But Lesic's wife Jasminka had no doubts. The X-ray shots of an old fracture to her husband's right arm and his dental records fitted perfectly with the forensic report.
She was absolutely sure when she recognised the set of keys found close to the body, and when one of them opened the doors of their flat.
"Tomislav gave to his homeland the most valuable possession -- his life. It is up to us to make it the way he wanted it to be: free, democratic and Christian," said one of the speakers.
"Let Tomislav and all our fathers rest in peace," said a young boy whose father went missing after the fall of Vukovar together with several hundred others.
Once a picturesque baroque Danube River town, Vukovar was completely demolished during a three-month siege by Serb irregulars and the Yugoslav army in August 1991.
Sobs from the crowd of some 500 people at the Zagreb crematorium interrupted emotional speeches. A detachment from the Croatian army fired shots in the air after the ceremony.
Many of the volunteers who were killed or went missing after the fall of Vukovar, which grew into a symbol of Croatia's fight for independence, came from Zagreb.
Lesic was treated in Vukovar hospital for injuries to his chest and arm which he sustained in a shell blast. Traces of bandages wrapped around his arm were found in the grave.
Earlier autopsies showed all Ovcara victims died of multiple gunshot wounds consistent with an execution-style killing, rather than from wounds that would have been incurred in battle.
The bodies were all male, ranging from teenagers to men in their 60s, and none was found in military uniform.

They were rounded up from Vukovar hospital by Yugoslav army troops, put on seven buses and driven away. They were never seen alive again. They are believed to have been killed on the Ovcara farm on November 21, 1991 and buried nearby.

The Hague tribunal has indicted three Yugoslav army officers for war crimes and crimes against humanity in connection with the Ovcara killings, but all are still free. The town and the area of Eastern Slavonia, captured by Serbs during their rebellion against Croatia's bid for independence from Yugoslavia, are scheduled to return to Zagreb rule by mid-July.
The area will be run by a U.N. administration until then.
